top_news.title: "India stands ready to work with ASEAN as reliable, equal partner": Rajnath Singh
top_news.summary: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Wednesday called for stronger defence cooperation between India and ASEAN countries, including joint research on maritime security, counter-drone systems, cyber defence and disaster response, stressing that regional challenges require collective action and practical solutions. Addressing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-India Defence Think Tank Forum in the national capital, Singh said the forum should move beyond an exchange of views and help identify practical steps that governments and institutions could jointly implement. "This forum grew out of my informal interaction with ASEAN defence ministers in Kuala Lumpur last year. I am pleased that this idea has now taken shape.I hope this meeting will do more than just exchange views. I hope it will help us identify practical steps that our governments and institutions can take together," Singh added. Highlighting the historical ties between India and Southeast Asia, the Defence Minister said their relationship was rooted in shared history, culture, trade and ideas, with maritime routes connecting their people for centuries. "For centuries, our people have connected through maritime routes across the Bay of Bengal, exchanging goods, knowledge, art, and traditions," he said. He noted that the influence of Indian philosophical and spiritual traditions could be seen in the temples, monuments, languages and cultural practices of the region. Ancient Indian kingdoms, including the Cholas and Pallavas, had maintained links with Southeast Asia through trade and maritime contact, he added. "Today, this civilizational bond provides a strong foundation for our modern partnership. As we work together for peace, stability, and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific, we draw strength from a history that reminds us that India and Southeast Asia have long been connected by the sea, by culture, and by the spirit of friendship. They are also a strong foundation of our future," Singh said. He said India and ASEAN shared an interest in peace, stability, prosperity and an open and inclusive Indo-Pacific, adding that ASEAN was central to India's Indo-Pacific vision. "India's Act East Policy, SAGAR and MAHASAGAR vision advocate open, multipolar cooperation, and we align these approaches through ASEAN-led mechanisms," he said, describing the Act East Policy as a long-term commitment to working with Southeast Asia as an equal partner. Referring to the changing regional security environment, Singh said strategic competition was growing and actions at sea were sometimes creating pressure and uncertainty. He also identified terrorism, cybercrime, piracy, trafficking, illegal fishing, climate-related disasters and risks to vital supply chains as challenges that crossed national borders."These challenges are often borderless. No country can address all of them alone," he said. The Defence Minister also stressed that countries should build trust, respect each other's sovereignty, follow international law and keep channels of dialogue open."Differences should be discussed early and peacefully before they become disputes. And we should support the regional order in which countries can work together without being forced to choose sides," he said. He said India attached great importance to ASEAN-led platforms such as the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus), adding that India's approach and ASEAN's outlook on the Indo-Pacific could complement each other. "We should strengthen cooperation, not create competition between regional forums," he said. On maritime security, Singh said the Indian Ocean and the waters of Southeast Asia formed a connected maritime space through which trade, energy, people and essential goods moved."The seas do not separate us. They connect us," he said, adding that keeping these waters safe was a shared responsibility. He identified maritime domain awareness, interoperability and cooperation in underwater awareness as key areas for ensuring a stable, rules-based maritime order. Singh said the designation of 2026 as the ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation provided an opportunity to translate shared interests into practical action."We should improve the sharing of maritime information, strengthen cooperation among our navies and coast guards, and build the ability to respond together to emergencies," he said. He also called for cooperation against piracy, trafficking, illegal fishing and other threats in accordance with international law. Encouraging experts at the forum to identify achievable measures, Singh proposed regular exchanges between maritime information centres, greater professional interaction among naval and coast guard personnel, and practical exercises focused on search and rescue, disaster relief and the protection of critical maritime infrastructure. He also called for examining gaps in underwater awareness and the ability to respond to activities that fall below the threshold of open conflict. The Defence Minister said cooperation should also prepare countries to deal with natural disasters, including cyclones, floods, rising sea levels and extreme weather, which could damage ports, disrupt trade and threaten lives and livelihoods. "Humanitarian assistance and disaster relief should therefore be a regular part of our defence dialogue. We can learn from one another, share best practices and improve coordination before a crisis occurs," he said. On defence technology, Singh said artificial intelligence, drones, cyber capabilities and space-based systems were becoming increasingly important in how countries protected themselves."Recent conflicts have also shown that relatively low-cost drones can challenge much more expensive defence systems. We need to respond with practical, affordable and adaptable solutions," he said. He stressed that innovation should not remain limited to large organisations, adding that startups, universities, research institutions and smaller companies could also contribute to defence capabilities. Singh cited India's Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) initiative and the Technology Development Fund as mechanisms that had created opportunities to collaborate with innovators on defence requirements. He invited think tanks to explore collaboration between Indian and ASEAN innovators on clearly defined challenges, including counter-drone systems, cyber defence, maritime surveillance and disaster response. "We should consider joint research projects, shared testing opportunities, exchanges among young researchers, and carefully designed innovation challenges," he said. He added that such cooperation should protect sensitive information, respect intellectual property rights and ensure the responsible sharing of technology."The aim should be to develop useful capabilities while strengthening trust between our countries," Singh said. Calling for greater defence industrial cooperation, the Minister said the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative was aimed at building stronger domestic capabilities but did not mean working in isolation. "Self-reliance doesn't mean working in isolation. It can create opportunities for trusted partners to design, build, maintain, and improve equipment together," he said. Singh said India was ready to explore cooperation with ASEAN partners in areas such as patrol vessels, radars, air defence systems, helicopters, drones and other technologies, according to the needs and priorities of individual countries. He called for moving beyond equipment purchases towards co-development, co-production, maintenance, repair, training and long-term technical support."These arrangements can build local skills, support industry, and make supply chains more reliable," he said. Singh also urged researchers to examine the factors necessary for successful partnerships, including clear requirements, reliable after-sales support, appropriate technology safeguards, fair sharing of responsibilities and benefits, and opportunities for local companies and skilled workers. "Our goal should be lasting partnership, not one-time transactions," he said. Highlighting the role of think tanks, Singh said governments needed sound analysis as well as ideas that could be translated into action."Think tanks can help us understand one another's concerns, identify common ground and offer options before challenges become crisis," he said. He proposed developing a joint India-ASEAN research agenda covering maritime security, cyber threats, emerging technologies, disaster response and defence industry cooperation. He also called for regular exchanges among researchers, including young scholars, through fellowships, visiting programmes and joint publications. Singh suggested identifying a small number of pilot projects, such as a tabletop exercise on maritime disaster response, a joint study on counter-drone solutions or a research project on secure maritime information sharing. He further called for promoting Track 1.5 and Track 2 dialogues to enable researchers, practitioners and policymakers to continue discussions between formal meetings. "Let us prepare a concise set of recommendations. After this forum, identify institutions that could take them forward and review progress at a future meeting.We should measure success not only by the quality of our discussions, but also by what we do afterwards," he added. Singh said the proposals were open to consideration and welcomed ideas from all participating countries, stressing that cooperation was strongest when it reflected the needs and experiences of every partner. "India seeks an Indo-Pacific where all countries, large and small, can make their own choices, protect their interests, and pursue development in peace," he said. He added that security was strengthened when countries built capacity together, respected international law and maintained trust through dialogue."India stands ready to work with ASEAN as a reliable and equal partner," Singh said. Concluding his address, the Defence Minister called on participants to translate shared understanding into practical cooperation, joint research and solutions that could improve regional security and the well-being of people. "Let this forum help us move from shared understanding to practical cooperation, from discussion to joint research and from joint research to solutions to improve the security and well-being of our people," he said. Singh wished participants productive discussions over the next two days and expressed hope that the forum would deepen ties and contribute to peace, stability and prosperity across the region. (ANI)

He added that such cooperation should protect sensitive information, respect intellectual property rights and ensure the responsible sharing of technology."The aim should be to develop useful capabilities while strengthening trust between our countries," Singh said. Calling for greater defence industrial cooperation, the Minister said the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative was aimed at building stronger domestic capabilities but did not mean working in isolation. "Self-reliance doesn't mean working in isolation. It can create opportunities for trusted partners to design, build, maintain, and improve equipment together," he said. Singh said India was ready to explore cooperation with ASEAN partners in areas such as patrol vessels, radars, air defence systems, helicopters, drones and other technologies, according to the needs and priorities of individual countries. He called for moving beyond equipment purchases towards co-development, co-production, maintenance, repair, training and long-term technical support."These arrangements can build local skills, support industry, and make supply chains more reliable," he said. Singh also urged researchers to examine the factors necessary for successful partnerships, including clear requirements, reliable after-sales support, appropriate technology safeguards, fair sharing of responsibilities and benefits, and opportunities for local companies and skilled workers. "Our goal should be lasting partnership, not one-time transactions," he said. Highlighting the role of think tanks, Singh said governments needed sound analysis as well as ideas that could be translated into action."Think tanks can help us understand one another's concerns, identify common ground and offer options before challenges become crisis," he said. He proposed developing a joint India-ASEAN research agenda covering maritime security, cyber threats, emerging technologies, disaster response and defence industry cooperation. He also called for regular exchanges among researchers, including young scholars, through fellowships, visiting programmes and joint publications. Singh suggested identifying a small number of pilot projects, such as a tabletop exercise on maritime disaster response, a joint study on counter-drone solutions or a research project on secure maritime information sharing. He further called for promoting Track 1.5 and Track 2 dialogues to enable researchers, practitioners and policymakers to continue discussions between formal meetings. "Let us prepare a concise set of recommendations. After this forum, identify institutions that could take them forward and review progress at a future meeting.We should measure success not only by the quality of our discussions, but also by what we do afterwards," he added. Singh said the proposals were open to consideration and welcomed ideas from all participating countries, stressing that cooperation was strongest when it reflected the needs and experiences of every partner. "India seeks an Indo-Pacific where all countries, large and small, can make their own choices, protect their interests, and pursue development in peace," he said. He added that security was strengthened when countries built capacity together, respected international law and maintained trust through dialogue."India stands ready to work with ASEAN as a reliable and equal partner," Singh said. Concluding his address, the Defence Minister called on participants to translate shared understanding into practical cooperation, joint research and solutions that could improve regional security and the well-being of people. "Let this forum help us move from shared understanding to practical cooperation, from discussion to joint research and from joint research to solutions to improve the security and well-being of our people," he said. Singh wished participants productive discussions over the next two days and expressed hope that the forum would deepen ties and contribute to peace, stability and prosperity across the region. (ANI)

top_news.title: Delhi HC enhances compensation for 74-year-old accident victim, says age cannot erase economic value of homemaker
top_news.summary: The Delhi High Court has held that advanced age cannot be a ground to presume that an elderly person has stopped contributing economically to the family, emphasising that unpaid household work and caregiving services rendered by older women must be recognised while determining compensation in motor accident cases. Justice Anish Dayal observed that compensation cannot be assessed on stereotypes or assumptions that a person ceases to contribute to the household merely because of age. The absence of monetary remuneration for domestic work cannot be allowed to benefit the person responsible for the accident or reduce the compensation payable to the victim. The court made the observations while enhancing the compensation payable to Ganga Devi, who was 74 years old when a bus accident in February 2019 crushed her legs, resulting in the amputation of her left leg below the knee and all the toes of her right foot. The High Court increased the compensation awarded to her by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) from Rs 14.42 lakh to Rs 20.79 lakh, an enhancement of Rs 6.37 lakh, along with interest at 7.5 per cent per annum from the date of filing of the claim petition. The court also awarded an additional Rs 1.30 lakh towards the cost of a further artificial limb and Rs 75,000 towards its maintenance, subject to the conditions specified in the judgment. "The absence of a monetary consideration cannot operate to the advantage of the tortfeasor or diminish the compensation otherwise payable to the injured claimant," Justice Dayal observed. The court rejected the approach of assessing an elderly homemaker as merely a dependent family member on account of her age. It noted that women above 70 years continue to perform household duties and provide care to grandchildren and other family members, contributions that often remain unrecognised because they do not generate a direct income. The judgment also highlighted the concept of "ageism", referring to prejudice and discrimination based on age, and stressed that such assumptions must not influence the assessment of compensation. The court said no age limit had been prescribed by the Supreme Court while recognising the economic value of unpaid care and domestic work for determining compensation. Introducing an age-based restriction would be contrary to the beneficial purpose of the Motor Vehicles Act and the requirement to award just and reasonable compensation. Ganga Devi was a homemaker and had never been formally employed. The MACT had declined to award compensation for loss of income or future earnings, reasoning that she was 74 years old, past the retirement age, and there was insufficient evidence to establish that she was performing household chores or looking after her grandchildren. The High Court found that this approach failed to adequately recognise the economic value of her contribution to the family. Taking into account her role as a homemaker in a joint family and her involvement in looking after her grandchildren, the court assessed her notional monthly income at Rs 16,962, corresponding to the minimum wages prescribed for a skilled worker in Delhi at the time of the accident. It held that the value of a homemaker's services cannot be denied merely because the work is unpaid or because the person has crossed a particular age. The court also noted that older persons are not merely recipients of care from younger family members but often provide substantial assistance themselves. Such contributions, including childcare and household management, have an identifiable economic value because families would otherwise have to incur expenses to obtain similar services. The court noted that Ganga Devi had suffered 74 per cent permanent physical disability in relation to both lower limbs. However, it clarified that physical disability and functional disability cannot automatically be treated as identical. Assessing the impact of her injuries on her ability to perform household activities and provide services to her family, the court fixed her functional disability at 50 per cent. It held that the assessment had to take into account her age, the nature of the work she performed before the accident and the extent to which her injuries restricted her ability to continue those activities. The court also rejected the argument that a claimant above 70 years of age could not be awarded compensation for future loss by applying the multiplier method. It held that the absence of a separate category for persons above 70 years in the multiplier table could not mean that their future losses were incapable of calculation. Applying a multiplier of five, the court awarded 5,08,860 towards loss of future income. It additionally awarded Rs 50,886 towards loss of income for three months, considering the prolonged treatment and repeated hospitalisations that prevented her from performing her usual household activities. The High Court increased the compensation towards attendant charges from Rs 50,000 to Rs 5 lakh, observing that the absence of evidence of a formally paid attendant did not, by itself, disentitle an injured person from compensation. It noted that assistance could be provided by family members without any payment being made to them, but such gratuitous assistance could not be disregarded while determining just compensation. At the same time, the court distinguished Ganga Devi's case from one involving 100 per cent functional disability and a requirement for round-the-clock assistance. It noted that the artificial limb could enable her to undertake some daily activities independently, while her age and permanent disability would nevertheless increase her need for assistance. The court also increased compensation for pain and suffering from Rs 75,000 to Rs 1 lakh, considering the nature of her injuries, the amputations and the impact of the accident at her advanced age. The court said the assumption of a life expectancy of 70 years, used in earlier judgments concerning artificial limbs, could not be treated as an absolute limit for a claimant who had already crossed that age. Referring to Supreme Court decisions recognising the need for replacement of prosthetic limbs, the court observed that a claimant's actual requirements must be considered rather than excluding them from compensation merely because they have crossed the assumed life expectancy. It awarded Rs 1.30 lakh towards one further artificial limb and Rs 75,000 towards maintenance. The amount for the artificial limb is to be kept in an interest-bearing fixed deposit and released upon production of the required purchase invoice and proof of payment to a reputed vendor. Any unutilised amount, along with accrued interest, is to be refunded to the insurance company upon an appropriate application. The enhanced compensation of Rs 6,37,307, along with interest at 7.5 per cent per annum from the date of filing of the claim petition, has been directed to be deposited before the MACT within four weeks. The court further directed that Rs 1,37,307 be released to Ganga Devi within two weeks thereafter, while the remaining enhanced amount and accrued interest are to be placed in fixed deposits with staggered maturities. (ANI)

articles.title: "India stands ready to work with ASEAN as reliable, equal partner": Rajnath Singh
articles.summary: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Wednesday called for stronger defence cooperation between India and ASEAN countries, including joint research on maritime security, counter-drone systems, cyber defence and disaster response, stressing that regional challenges require collective action and practical solutions. Addressing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-India Defence Think Tank Forum in the national capital, Singh said the forum should move beyond an exchange of views and help identify practical steps that governments and institutions could jointly implement. "This forum grew out of my informal interaction with ASEAN defence ministers in Kuala Lumpur last year. I am pleased that this idea has now taken shape.I hope this meeting will do more than just exchange views. I hope it will help us identify practical steps that our governments and institutions can take together," Singh added. Highlighting the historical ties between India and Southeast Asia, the Defence Minister said their relationship was rooted in shared history, culture, trade and ideas, with maritime routes connecting their people for centuries. "For centuries, our people have connected through maritime routes across the Bay of Bengal, exchanging goods, knowledge, art, and traditions," he said. He noted that the influence of Indian philosophical and spiritual traditions could be seen in the temples, monuments, languages and cultural practices of the region. Ancient Indian kingdoms, including the Cholas and Pallavas, had maintained links with Southeast Asia through trade and maritime contact, he added. "Today, this civilizational bond provides a strong foundation for our modern partnership. As we work together for peace, stability, and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific, we draw strength from a history that reminds us that India and Southeast Asia have long been connected by the sea, by culture, and by the spirit of friendship. They are also a strong foundation of our future," Singh said. He said India and ASEAN shared an interest in peace, stability, prosperity and an open and inclusive Indo-Pacific, adding that ASEAN was central to India's Indo-Pacific vision. "India's Act East Policy, SAGAR and MAHASAGAR vision advocate open, multipolar cooperation, and we align these approaches through ASEAN-led mechanisms," he said, describing the Act East Policy as a long-term commitment to working with Southeast Asia as an equal partner. Referring to the changing regional security environment, Singh said strategic competition was growing and actions at sea were sometimes creating pressure and uncertainty. He also identified terrorism, cybercrime, piracy, trafficking, illegal fishing, climate-related disasters and risks to vital supply chains as challenges that crossed national borders."These challenges are often borderless. No country can address all of them alone," he said. The Defence Minister also stressed that countries should build trust, respect each other's sovereignty, follow international law and keep channels of dialogue open."Differences should be discussed early and peacefully before they become disputes. And we should support the regional order in which countries can work together without being forced to choose sides," he said. He said India attached great importance to ASEAN-led platforms such as the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus), adding that India's approach and ASEAN's outlook on the Indo-Pacific could complement each other. "We should strengthen cooperation, not create competition between regional forums," he said. On maritime security, Singh said the Indian Ocean and the waters of Southeast Asia formed a connected maritime space through which trade, energy, people and essential goods moved."The seas do not separate us. They connect us," he said, adding that keeping these waters safe was a shared responsibility. He identified maritime domain awareness, interoperability and cooperation in underwater awareness as key areas for ensuring a stable, rules-based maritime order. Singh said the designation of 2026 as the ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation provided an opportunity to translate shared interests into practical action."We should improve the sharing of maritime information, strengthen cooperation among our navies and coast guards, and build the ability to respond together to emergencies," he said. He also called for cooperation against piracy, trafficking, illegal fishing and other threats in accordance with international law. Encouraging experts at the forum to identify achievable measures, Singh proposed regular exchanges between maritime information centres, greater professional interaction among naval and coast guard personnel, and practical exercises focused on search and rescue, disaster relief and the protection of critical maritime infrastructure. He also called for examining gaps in underwater awareness and the ability to respond to activities that fall below the threshold of open conflict. The Defence Minister said cooperation should also prepare countries to deal with natural disasters, including cyclones, floods, rising sea levels and extreme weather, which could damage ports, disrupt trade and threaten lives and livelihoods. "Humanitarian assistance and disaster relief should therefore be a regular part of our defence dialogue. We can learn from one another, share best practices and improve coordination before a crisis occurs," he said. On defence technology, Singh said artificial intelligence, drones, cyber capabilities and space-based systems were becoming increasingly important in how countries protected themselves."Recent conflicts have also shown that relatively low-cost drones can challenge much more expensive defence systems. We need to respond with practical, affordable and adaptable solutions," he said. He stressed that innovation should not remain limited to large organisations, adding that startups, universities, research institutions and smaller companies could also contribute to defence capabilities. Singh cited India's Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) initiative and the Technology Development Fund as mechanisms that had created opportunities to collaborate with innovators on defence requirements. He invited think tanks to explore collaboration between Indian and ASEAN innovators on clearly defined challenges, including counter-drone systems, cyber defence, maritime surveillance and disaster response. "We should consider joint research projects, shared testing opportunities, exchanges among young researchers, and carefully designed innovation challenges," he said. He added that such cooperation should protect sensitive information, respect intellectual property rights and ensure the responsible sharing of technology."The aim should be to develop useful capabilities while strengthening trust between our countries," Singh said. Calling for greater defence industrial cooperation, the Minister said the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative was aimed at building stronger domestic capabilities but did not mean working in isolation. "Self-reliance doesn't mean working in isolation. It can create opportunities for trusted partners to design, build, maintain, and improve equipment together," he said. Singh said India was ready to explore cooperation with ASEAN partners in areas such as patrol vessels, radars, air defence systems, helicopters, drones and other technologies, according to the needs and priorities of individual countries. He called for moving beyond equipment purchases towards co-development, co-production, maintenance, repair, training and long-term technical support."These arrangements can build local skills, support industry, and make supply chains more reliable," he said. Singh also urged researchers to examine the factors necessary for successful partnerships, including clear requirements, reliable after-sales support, appropriate technology safeguards, fair sharing of responsibilities and benefits, and opportunities for local companies and skilled workers. "Our goal should be lasting partnership, not one-time transactions," he said. Highlighting the role of think tanks, Singh said governments needed sound analysis as well as ideas that could be translated into action."Think tanks can help us understand one another's concerns, identify common ground and offer options before challenges become crisis," he said. He proposed developing a joint India-ASEAN research agenda covering maritime security, cyber threats, emerging technologies, disaster response and defence industry cooperation. He also called for regular exchanges among researchers, including young scholars, through fellowships, visiting programmes and joint publications. Singh suggested identifying a small number of pilot projects, such as a tabletop exercise on maritime disaster response, a joint study on counter-drone solutions or a research project on secure maritime information sharing. He further called for promoting Track 1.5 and Track 2 dialogues to enable researchers, practitioners and policymakers to continue discussions between formal meetings. "Let us prepare a concise set of recommendations. After this forum, identify institutions that could take them forward and review progress at a future meeting.We should measure success not only by the quality of our discussions, but also by what we do afterwards," he added. Singh said the proposals were open to consideration and welcomed ideas from all participating countries, stressing that cooperation was strongest when it reflected the needs and experiences of every partner. "India seeks an Indo-Pacific where all countries, large and small, can make their own choices, protect their interests, and pursue development in peace," he said. He added that security was strengthened when countries built capacity together, respected international law and maintained trust through dialogue."India stands ready to work with ASEAN as a reliable and equal partner," Singh said. Concluding his address, the Defence Minister called on participants to translate shared understanding into practical cooperation, joint research and solutions that could improve regional security and the well-being of people. "Let this forum help us move from shared understanding to practical cooperation, from discussion to joint research and from joint research to solutions to improve the security and well-being of our people," he said. Singh wished participants productive discussions over the next two days and expressed hope that the forum would deepen ties and contribute to peace, stability and prosperity across the region. (ANI)

articles.title: Delhi HC enhances compensation for 74-year-old accident victim, says age cannot erase economic value of homemaker
articles.summary: The Delhi High Court has held that advanced age cannot be a ground to presume that an elderly person has stopped contributing economically to the family, emphasising that unpaid household work and caregiving services rendered by older women must be recognised while determining compensation in motor accident cases. Justice Anish Dayal observed that compensation cannot be assessed on stereotypes or assumptions that a person ceases to contribute to the household merely because of age. The absence of monetary remuneration for domestic work cannot be allowed to benefit the person responsible for the accident or reduce the compensation payable to the victim. The court made the observations while enhancing the compensation payable to Ganga Devi, who was 74 years old when a bus accident in February 2019 crushed her legs, resulting in the amputation of her left leg below the knee and all the toes of her right foot. The High Court increased the compensation awarded to her by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) from Rs 14.42 lakh to Rs 20.79 lakh, an enhancement of Rs 6.37 lakh, along with interest at 7.5 per cent per annum from the date of filing of the claim petition. The court also awarded an additional Rs 1.30 lakh towards the cost of a further artificial limb and Rs 75,000 towards its maintenance, subject to the conditions specified in the judgment. "The absence of a monetary consideration cannot operate to the advantage of the tortfeasor or diminish the compensation otherwise payable to the injured claimant," Justice Dayal observed. The court rejected the approach of assessing an elderly homemaker as merely a dependent family member on account of her age. It noted that women above 70 years continue to perform household duties and provide care to grandchildren and other family members, contributions that often remain unrecognised because they do not generate a direct income. The judgment also highlighted the concept of "ageism", referring to prejudice and discrimination based on age, and stressed that such assumptions must not influence the assessment of compensation. The court said no age limit had been prescribed by the Supreme Court while recognising the economic value of unpaid care and domestic work for determining compensation. Introducing an age-based restriction would be contrary to the beneficial purpose of the Motor Vehicles Act and the requirement to award just and reasonable compensation. Ganga Devi was a homemaker and had never been formally employed. The MACT had declined to award compensation for loss of income or future earnings, reasoning that she was 74 years old, past the retirement age, and there was insufficient evidence to establish that she was performing household chores or looking after her grandchildren. The High Court found that this approach failed to adequately recognise the economic value of her contribution to the family. Taking into account her role as a homemaker in a joint family and her involvement in looking after her grandchildren, the court assessed her notional monthly income at Rs 16,962, corresponding to the minimum wages prescribed for a skilled worker in Delhi at the time of the accident. It held that the value of a homemaker's services cannot be denied merely because the work is unpaid or because the person has crossed a particular age. The court also noted that older persons are not merely recipients of care from younger family members but often provide substantial assistance themselves. Such contributions, including childcare and household management, have an identifiable economic value because families would otherwise have to incur expenses to obtain similar services. The court noted that Ganga Devi had suffered 74 per cent permanent physical disability in relation to both lower limbs. However, it clarified that physical disability and functional disability cannot automatically be treated as identical. Assessing the impact of her injuries on her ability to perform household activities and provide services to her family, the court fixed her functional disability at 50 per cent. It held that the assessment had to take into account her age, the nature of the work she performed before the accident and the extent to which her injuries restricted her ability to continue those activities. The court also rejected the argument that a claimant above 70 years of age could not be awarded compensation for future loss by applying the multiplier method. It held that the absence of a separate category for persons above 70 years in the multiplier table could not mean that their future losses were incapable of calculation. Applying a multiplier of five, the court awarded 5,08,860 towards loss of future income. It additionally awarded Rs 50,886 towards loss of income for three months, considering the prolonged treatment and repeated hospitalisations that prevented her from performing her usual household activities. The High Court increased the compensation towards attendant charges from Rs 50,000 to Rs 5 lakh, observing that the absence of evidence of a formally paid attendant did not, by itself, disentitle an injured person from compensation. It noted that assistance could be provided by family members without any payment being made to them, but such gratuitous assistance could not be disregarded while determining just compensation. At the same time, the court distinguished Ganga Devi's case from one involving 100 per cent functional disability and a requirement for round-the-clock assistance. It noted that the artificial limb could enable her to undertake some daily activities independently, while her age and permanent disability would nevertheless increase her need for assistance. The court also increased compensation for pain and suffering from Rs 75,000 to Rs 1 lakh, considering the nature of her injuries, the amputations and the impact of the accident at her advanced age. The court said the assumption of a life expectancy of 70 years, used in earlier judgments concerning artificial limbs, could not be treated as an absolute limit for a claimant who had already crossed that age. Referring to Supreme Court decisions recognising the need for replacement of prosthetic limbs, the court observed that a claimant's actual requirements must be considered rather than excluding them from compensation merely because they have crossed the assumed life expectancy. It awarded Rs 1.30 lakh towards one further artificial limb and Rs 75,000 towards maintenance. The amount for the artificial limb is to be kept in an interest-bearing fixed deposit and released upon production of the required purchase invoice and proof of payment to a reputed vendor. Any unutilised amount, along with accrued interest, is to be refunded to the insurance company upon an appropriate application. The enhanced compensation of Rs 6,37,307, along with interest at 7.5 per cent per annum from the date of filing of the claim petition, has been directed to be deposited before the MACT within four weeks. The court further directed that Rs 1,37,307 be released to Ganga Devi within two weeks thereafter, while the remaining enhanced amount and accrued interest are to be placed in fixed deposits with staggered maturities. (ANI)
